questions.title: When does a 'procedural right in vacuo' fail to confer Article III standing?
questions.question_body: I'm reading the second section where the court discusses Article III standing. The court cites *Summers v. Earth Island Inst.* to say that a 'procedural right in vacuo' is insufficient. AFL argues it has a procedural right to an investigation under § 1216. How does this doctrine work specifically when the defendant (OSC) is statutorily mandated to investigate FOIA violations, but the plaintiff's injury is non-concrete? Does the 'concrete interest' requirement mean the plaintiff must have a private concrete interest unrelated to the procedural right itself?

questions.title: Why is the causal chain between an OSC investigation and DOJ record production considered too speculative?
questions.question_body: In the second standing theory analysis, the court outlines a speculative chain: OSC investigates -> OSC seeks corrective action -> MSPB sanctions employees -> DOJ produces records. The court cites *FDA v. All. for Hippocratic Med.* to dismiss this. If OSC is the defendant in the lawsuit, why does the court allow the possibility of DOE/MSPB discretion to break the causal chain? Does a violation of the law (in DFA investigation) need to compel the other parties to act immediately, and does OSC lack the enforcement power to do so unilaterally?

questions.title: Why does OSC's discretion over § 1214 notice requirements in § 1216 cases prevent informational standing?
questions.question_body: AFL's second claim rests on the idea that it is 'informationally entitled' to OSC notices if OSC were investigating under § 1214. However, the court notes OSC's discretion to ignore § 1214's procedural requirements when acting under § 1216. If OSC has discretion to not provide notices, AFL argues it has no injury. Why does having the *possibility* of not receiving notes constitute no injury of fact? If the statute mandates OSC to investigate, shouldn't the potential realization of rights be the injury?

questions.title: How does the *Hecate Energy* test on redressability apply to this standing claim?
questions.question_body: The opinion references *Hecate Energy LLC v. FERC* (2025) regarding redressability, stating a judgment must 'very likely spur the next steps necessary to redress' the injury. We've previously seen redressability arguments where the defendant has the discretion to act. Here, if OSC wins or loses, a court order 'may compel next steps' by OSC, but OSC's discretion hides between OSC and the redressable injury. Is *Hecate Energy* clarifying that courts cannot force OSC to use enforcement powers against other agencies?

questions.title: Why do standing issues preclude the court from ruling on the substantive 'shall' language in 5 U.S.C. § 1216?
questions.question_body: The district court had already ruled that § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) does not limit OSC power under § 1216. The appellate court said it didn't need to decide this because AFL lacks standing. If OSC is statutorily forbidden from refusing to investigate, would AFL have a cause of action? Is the court preempting its own interpretation of the statute because standing doctrine is a jurisdictional limit? Why is the statutory interpretation not enough to grant standing if I have the right to relief?

questions.title: What is the relationship between 'independent actors' and OSC's role in redressing FOIA requests?
questions.question_body: The court repeatedly mentions that DOJ cannot be bound by OSC's judgment. The text cites 'principles' from *Haaland v. Brackeen* (2023) regarding injunctive relief not binding non-parties. Since ACJ is suing OSC, not DOJ, does this mean OSC's enforcement power is limited to internal discipline? Does the absence of oversight power over DOJ create the 'redressability' barrier, or does the lack of private enforcement against a federal body create a constitutional limit on adjudication generally?
